explanations.answer: They obey the voice of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Zerubbabel, Joshua and all the remnant of the people "…obeyed the voice of the LORD their God and the words of the prophet Haggai…" (Haggai 1:12). They hear it, and they obey.

explanations.answer: They return to their own houses
explanations.explanation: I get why you picked it, friend. The LORD had just told them they were each busy with their own house (Haggai 1:9), so going back there sounds like the natural next step. But Haggai 1:12 says they obeyed the voice of the LORD their God. They heard the whole message and they listened.

explanations.answer: They wait until the time has come
explanations.explanation: Waiting is a smooth move, I'll give you that. In Haggai 1:2 the people had said, "The time has not yet come…" But this time the text says they obeyed the voice of the LORD, and it doesn't say they waited for anything (Haggai 1:12).

Yes, sent! The people obeyed Haggai's words "…because the LORD their God had sent him." (Haggai 1:12). They didn't hear one man's opinion. They heard a messenger with a message from the LORD, and they treated it that way.
I see why you picked it, friend. But the word in the text is "sent." The people obeyed Haggai because the LORD their God had sent him (Haggai 1:12). It's about who stood behind the prophet.
I can see why you'd pick it, baker. But the verse says they obeyed because the LORD their God had "sent" him (Haggai 1:12). The reason the text gives is who sent Haggai.

There it is. "I am with you…" declares the LORD (Haggai 1:13). Haggai delivers those four little words to the people who just obeyed. I think that's about the best thing you could hear right when you're about to roll up your sleeves.
Ooh, a deadline! Sounds like something a foreman would say. But the text has no deadline in it. The LORD says, "I am with you…" (Haggai 1:13), and that's the whole message.
Bigger! I like the ambition, friend, but that's not in this passage. The message is short: "I am with you…" declares the LORD (Haggai 1:13). Nothing about size, only about Him being with them.

Right on, baker. "…the LORD stirred the spirit of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah…" (Haggai 1:14). Notice who does the stirring. The governor didn't pump himself up with a speech in the mirror.

Haggai did bring the message, so I see the thinking. But the verse names who stirred the spirit, and it says "…the LORD stirred the spirit of Zerubbabel…" (Haggai 1:14). Haggai delivers the words, and the stirring comes from the LORD.

Joshua is right there in the verse, friend, so it's an easy mix-up. Joshua, the high priest, gets his own spirit stirred too (Haggai 1:14). But the one doing the stirring for both of them is the LORD.

Not quite, baker, and it's a sneaky one because the governor goes first in the verse. The text says the LORD stirred the spirit of Zerubbabel, "…and the spirit of Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, as well as the spirit of all the remnant of the people." (Haggai 1:14). The whole crowd gets stirred, not just the governor.

That's right, friend. The LORD stirred the spirit of Zerubbabel, and also the spirit of Joshua the high priest and "…the spirit of all the remnant of the people." (Haggai 1:14). Nobody got left on the sidelines. Governor, priest and people all get stirred.

Yes, begin! The text says "…they came and began the work on the house of the LORD of Hosts, their God…" (Haggai 1:14). The LORD had called His house a ruin (Haggai 1:9), and now the work on it starts. Every big job has a first day, and this is theirs.
Finishing is the fun part, I know. But the verse says they "began" the work on the house of the LORD of Hosts (Haggai 1:14). This verse is about the start of the work, not the end.

Inspecting sounds like something a committee would do, friend, with clipboards and serious faces. But the text says they came and "began" the work (Haggai 1:14). Begin is the word in the verse, and inspect isn't in it.
That's the one, baker. The work begins "…in the second year of King Darius." (Haggai 1:15). The text pins down the day and the year, and I love a passage that keeps good records.
Cyrus, king of Persia, is a real king in the Bible (Ezra 1:1), so it's a fair guess. But Haggai 1:15 says the work began in the second year of King Darius. Cyrus isn't named in this passage.
Artaxerxes is a big name, friend, and it sounds like it belongs in a story about rebuilding. But this passage names a different king. The work begins in the second year of King Darius (Haggai 1:15).
